extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotle / students of moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Exegesis of Aristotle's account of virtues and vices (especially courage, self-mastery/temperance, liberality, magnificence) describing each virtue as a mean between excess and defect and listing variant/false forms. Useful for analyzing or applying Nicomachean Ethics Book IV (and preceding discussion of courage/self-mastery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as a mean state
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is a mean state between excess and defect with respect to a particular object-matter (e.g., fear/confidence for courage; pleasures for self-mastery; wealth for liberality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each virtue is defined relative to its object-matter and is the correct intermediate disposition (the right amount, toward the right objects, at the right times, and for the right motives). Vices are the corresponding excesses and deficiencies; understanding virtue requires identifying the specific object-matter and how to hit the mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage (bravery) as a mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is the mean state in respect of objects inspiring boldness or fear: the Brave man stands in the right relation to fear and confidence and chooses to withstand danger because it is honourable or because not to do so is base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage concerns more the objects of fear than confidence and involves enduring painful/dangerous things for honourable ends; the Brave are composed before danger and sharp in action. The Brave man resists fear when appropriate and chooses honour even at personal cost; dying to escape poverty, love, or mere pain is cowardly, not brave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cowardice (defect regarding courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowardice is an excess of fear (or wrong fear): the coward fears wrong objects, in wrong ways, and is deficient in confidence; often fainthearted and fearful of many things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cowardice shows itself by fleeing true dangers and by being unduly shaken by pains; it is distinct from involuntary fear in particular cases because it characterizes the habitual response (the disposition) of the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rashness (excess regarding courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rashness is an excess of confidence or boldness: rash persons are precipitate, eager before danger, but often fall away when danger truly appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rashness contrasts with true bravery: rash people act without the proper deliberation or sense of honour; they appear bold but lack the stable, honour-driven resolve of the Brave man and often fail under real pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variants/false forms of Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Several dispositions resemble courage but are not true courage: (1) civic/honor-driven bravery, (2) obedience under compulsion, (3) experience/skill-based bravery, (4) animal spirit/impetuosity, and (5) ignorance-driven bravery; anger, thirst for revenge, and sanguine overconfidence also mimic bravery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes these as follows: civic/honor-based courage arises from shame and desire of honour (close to true courage but sometimes lower); compulsion (soldiers under commanders) acts from fear of pain/disgrace and is inferior; skill/experience gives a show of courage (trained troops may flee when danger exceeds resources); animal spirit (impetuosity, pain-induced ferocity) and anger-driven fighting lack choice/motive and thus are not true courage; ignorance causes temporary show of bravery that collapses when error is revealed. True courage requires moral choice and the proper motive (honour), not mere habit, training, impulse, or ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and the role of pain, honour, and sudden fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage involves enduring pain and is especially praised in sudden fear because it reflects a fixed habit rather than calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True courage accepts that even a brave man will feel the pain and fear of death; the virtue is choosing honour despite those pains. Being fearless under sudden alarm shows more genuine courage than calculated bravery in anticipated dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfected Self-Mastery (temperance) as a mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfected self-mastery is the mean state regarding pleasures (chiefly bodily pleasures); the perfectly self-mastering person desires pleasures in right measure, at right times, and in right ways in accordance with reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This virtue primarily concerns bodily pleasures (especially touch and taste). Mental pleasures (love of honour, learning) and pleasures of sight/hearing/smell are less central. The temperate person neither indulges in base pleasures nor is pained by their absence; appetitive impulses are obedient to reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of self-control (incontinence/vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice of being destitute of self-control is an excess in relation to pleasures: seeking wrong objects, taking pleasure excessively or at wrong times, and being consumed by desire (e.g., gluttony, lust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This vice is often more voluntary than cowardice because pleasure is an object of choice; particular indulgences are voluntary acts that form a habit. Such persons are compared to children: desire is insatiable and unchastened, leading to loss of reason and increasing vice. Pleasure can paradoxically cause pain (desire itself is accompanied by pain when frustrated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of pleasures and senses (object-matter for self-mastery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures divide into mental and bodily; among bodily pleasures, touch and taste are the primary object-matter of self-mastery; pleasures of sight/hearing/smell are less central or only incidentally relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because animals share touch and taste pleasures, excess in these marks a brutish, servile disposition. Taste more narrowly can be a cultivated discriminative sense (e.g., wine-tasting), while the sensual appetite for touch/consummatory pleasures signals lack of self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality (generosity) as a mean regarding wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality is the mean in respect of giving and receiving wealth: the liberal person gives to proper persons, in right proportion, at right times, from a motive of honour, and with right feeling (pleasure or at least no pain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberality concerns money and economically measured goods. The liberal give s in accordance with his means (proportionate generosity), does not receive from improper sources, refrains from asking or from careless keeping, and values wealth instrumentally as means to give. Proper giving is praiseworthy and valuable to the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prodigality (excess regarding wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prodigality is the excess of giving (and sometimes forbearing to receive) often done recklessly or to satisfy passions rather than honour; prodigals may give to improper people or for improper ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prodigality differs from pure vice in that it may be folly rather than baseness: prodigals give freely but not rightly (wrong recipients, wrong motives), and often must accept improper receipts later. It is more correctable than stinginess and may be cured by habituation or lack of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stinginess / illiberality (defect regarding wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stinginess is the defect in giving and/or an excess in receiving: those who are close-fisted, sparing, or who accept gain from improper sources are stingy/illiberal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms include those who give nothing (skinflints) and those who receive anything for base gain (usurers, brothel-keepers, thieves). Stinginess is widely prevalent and morally worse than prodigality because it refuses to benefit others and often submits to disgrace for small gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence (great-scale fitting expenditure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnificence is the virtue like liberality but pertaining to large-scale, fitting expenditure (public, expensive works); it is the mean with respect to magnitude and tasteful largeness of expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magnificent person spends on great works in due proportion and with attention to beauty and fittingness rather than mere cheapness or ostentation. Faults are meanness (defect) and vulgar profusion or want of taste (excess). Magnificence presupposes liberality and is motivated by honour; it seeks to make works appropriate and splendid rather than simply costly.
